item.title: UK advises against using any Saudi airport except Medina
item.description:
UK advises against using any Saudi airport except Medina

Submitted by Imran Mulla on Mon, 10/12/2026 - 09:12
The UK has further warned British nationals not to try and leave Saudi Arabia via airports in the country
An air traffic control tower is seen at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on 19 September 2026 (AFP)
Off

The British government has advised its citizens against all but essential travel to parts of Saudi Arabia, including Jeddah and Dammam, and to all airports in the country except Medina International Airport. 

The UK has further warned British nationals not to try and leave Saudi Arabia via airports in the country.

This comes after a fresh attack on a passenger terminal at Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, which killed at least one person and wounded 11.

Saturday's attack on the airport killed at least 13 people and wounded more than 300 - making it the deadliest strike on a Gulf country since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on 28 February.

Saudi Arabia's General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement that four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed in the attack. 

It was the third attack on the airport in a week, following earlier strikes that killed four people and damaged a Saudi commercial aircraft.

The British Foreign Office updated its official guidance on Sunday to advise UK nationals against "all but essential travel to all airports within Saudi Arabia except for Medina International Airport", as well as "all but essential travel to Aseer province, Riyadh province, Najran province, Jizan province and the cities of Taif, Jeddah and Dammam".

Houthi forces warn against use of Saudi airports following Riyadh attack
Read More »

The Foreign Office further advised against all travel to within 10km of the border with Yemen.

"As an alternative to airports within Saudi Arabia," the Foreign Office said British nationals wishing to depart Saudi Arabia should consider options to travel by land to neighbouring countries and fly from there.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree warned travellers, airlines and shipping companies not to use Saudi airports and airspace, saying they are “exposed to targeting and a theatre for operations by our forces”, with the exception of the airports of Mecca and Medina.

Saree said Houthi forces carried out several operations against King Khalid airport on Saturday, “resulting in the disruption of air traffic at the airport and its complete closure”.

He also listed King Fahd Airport in Dammam, an Aramco-affiliated petrol station and a refinery in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Region among the targets.

'Dangerous escalation'

The latest attacks mark a significant escalation in the conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi movement in Yemen, with renewed fighting and a Saudi-led military offensive against the group. 

British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting condemned Saturday's airport attack as a "dangerous escalation" and "completely contemptible action".

Meanwhile in Yemen, air strikes have been reported on the Hamdan district in Sanaa and two more strikes on al-Zurbi Road in the Hayfan district in Taiz, according to Sanaa-based media. 

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan activate Mecca Pact amid war with Houthis
Read More »

Missile attacks were also reported on the border district of al-Dhaher in Saada province. No casualties have been reported so far. 

The US State Department has urged American citizens to take "extreme caution" when travelling through airports in Saudi Arabia, amid renewed attacks.

"U.S. government employees working in Saudi Arabia require special authorization to use the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, as well as the airports in Jeddah and Dammam," its official account on X said.

"Please take extreme caution when using all major airports in Saudi Arabia. U.S. citizens should be aware of potential flight cancellations, airspace closures, and travel disruptions."

Amid the escalation, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke over the phone to his Saudi counterpart Faisal bin Farhan.

According to Iranian state media, Araghchi said Iran was ready to help start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen. 

He expressed concern over escalating tensions, and insisted that a "military approach and ignoring a political solution will further complicate the current situation".

Araghchi also further stressed that crisis in the region "have no military solution", adding that Tehran is "ready to provide any assistance to help start dialogue between Saudi Arabia and Yemen and to help achieve a political solution".

item.title: Pakistani national killed, 11 wounded as Riyadh airport hit by Houthi strike
item.description:
A fresh Houthi strike hit Riyadh’s international airport on Sunday, killing one person — a Pakistani resident — and wounding 11 others, a day after another deadly attack claimed by the Yemeni group forced authorities to suspend operations there.

Saturday’s attack, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, was a sharp escalation in the Yemen war, where Riyadh has long militarily supported the internationally recognised government against the Houthis.

The group on Sunday claimed multiple attacks over the last 24 hours, including on the airport, and threatened to keep targeting the kingdom’s transit hubs, calling them “a theatre of operations for our forces”.

Hours later, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group reported that a projectile struck King Khalid International Airport, sparking a fire.

Air defences also intercepted a missile nearby, it added.

The fresh attack on the airport killed one person — a Pakistani resident — and wounded 11 others, Saudi Arabia’s civil aviation authority said on X.

Authorities have extended the closure of the airport by 24 hours until 2100 GMT (2am PKT) on Monday, the tracking site Flightradar24 said on the same platform.

AFP journalists and locals reported hearing multiple blasts in the Saudi capital on Sunday.

“The birds went into a frenzy after the sound. The whole house shook,” said one resident of the Al-Aarid neighbourhood in the north of the city.

The civil aviation authority also reported another attack on Dammam airport in the east — which the Houthis also said they had targeted — a day after the Saudi coalition reported a projectile landing nearby.

Shortly afterwards, the coalition reported shooting down a drone, also in the east.

It said early on Monday that it had also “intercepted and destroyed” a Houthi ballistic missile heading for the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait, home to a major military base.

‘Full-fledged war crime’

The Houthis have stepped up their attacks on the Riyadh airport — where three people were also killed on Thursday — as well as on other key targets in the world’s top crude oil exporter.

And although Saudi Arabia has poured billions into its military, Houthi attacks continue to slip through.

“Saudi air defences have been able to intercept some Houthi missile and drone attacks, but Saudi Arabia is so large that it’s simply impossible for them to consistently defend themselves against Houthi attacks,” said Thomas Juneau, security analyst at Ottawa University.

The anti-Houthi coalition called Saturday’s attack a “full-fledged war crime” and vowed to “respond decisively”.

Houthi media reported two Saudi strikes in Yemen’s Houthi-controlled Sanaa governorate on Sunday.

Saturday’s attack drew condemnation from the United Nations and leaders around the world, including US President Donald Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes against the Houthis.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose country does not have diplomatic relations with Saudi Arabia, also denounced the “horrific terrorist attack”.

Four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshis, one American, one Egyptian, one Jordanian, one Syrian, one Palestinian and one Sudanese were killed, the civil aviation authority said, with 309 wounded.

The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia also said one of its citizens died on Sunday after being wounded the day before.

A Riyadh-based Western diplomat told AFP the official number of injured may not give a full picture, as it did not appear to include those with minor wounds.

Operations suspended

Authorities suspended operations at the airport into Sunday, a senior aviation source said, with air traffic monitor Flightradar24 saying the closure was extended until 21:00 GMT (2am PKT on Monday).

A second aviation source confirmed the halt in operations “until further notice”, adding radar and communications equipment was damaged and runways needed to be assessed.

Witnesses to Saturday’s strike described chaos in the aftermath.

“People who were in Terminal 3 started running towards us,” a 32-year-old Riyadh resident told AFP.

“Some had lost a hand or an arm. People were running while carrying injured people, covered in blood.”

The attack prompted health officials to activate a rare mass call-up of doctors, a medical source said.

The US, Canadian, German and Spanish embassies in Saudi Arabia have warned their citizens to avoid Riyadh airport, while Australia urged its citizens on Sunday to stay indoors altogether and “shelter in place”.

The Houthis also claimed to have targeted the Dammam airport, whose official website on Sunday showed many flights — both departures and arrivals — were delayed.

‘Rewrite the rules’

Saturday’s airport strike, on the eve of Saudi Arabia’s high-profile convention and entertainment season, was the deadliest attack in the kingdom since a 2015 suicide bombing.

With the summer heat subsiding, October also usually marks the beginning of the high season for Umrah pilgrims, with millions of Muslims from across the world flocking to Makkah.

Saudi Arabia leads an international coalition that has supported Yemen’s government militarily since 2015, including by seeking to exert control over Yemeni airspace and the airport in the Houthi-held capital Sanaa.

Ottawa University’s Juneau said the Houthis now “want to rewrite the rules of the game”.

“They want to do to Saudi Arabia what Saudi Arabia does to them,” he said.

“So if their airport in Sanaa has to be closed because of the Saudi air embargo, they want to do the same thing to Saudi Arabia.”

On the ground in Yemen, Saudi-supported government forces were advancing in their counter-offensive against the Houthis around the Bab al-Mandab strait, a key shipping route, military sources said on Saturday.

The Houthis claimed to have repelled them.

Claims by both sides have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast on the ground and access for journalists difficult.

Secretariat to be relocated to old trade fair venue, new road to be built
item.description:
As the Secretariat will be relocated to Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, there will be no new buildings inside the Secretariat located on Abdul Gani Road in the capital.

The government made a policy decision last Wednesday to relocate the Secretariat in a meeting presided over by Prime Minister Tarique Rahman.

Top officials from the Ministry of Housing and Public Works, the Public Works Department, and the Department of Architecture were present at the meeting held at the Prime Minister's Office.

The following day, the Ministry of Housing and Public Works sent a letter to the Planning Commission to include a project for relocating the Secretariat in the Annual Development Programme (ADP).

An inter-ministerial meeting on this project is expected to be held at the Planning Commission next week.

According to a related source, the government aims to commence the project work as soon as possible and achieve visible progress during its tenure.

When contacted, the Chief Architect of the Department of Architecture, Asifur Rahman Bhuiyan, who attended the meeting, told Prothom Alo that three separate designs were presented by the Department of Architecture for relocating the Secretariat to Sher-e-Bangla Nagar. Everyone agreed to finalise one of the designs.

Architect Asifur Rahman Bhuiyan said that the project will be developed based on this design. The designs will also be presented at the meeting of the Executive Committee of the National Economic Council (ECNEC).

Past initiatives, no progress

According to information from the Ministry of Housing and Public Works, several initiatives to relocate the Secretariat to Sher-e-Bangla Nagar were taken during various periods, including under the Awami League government that was ousted in the July uprising.

In 2015, a project worth Tk 22.09 billion was initiated to relocate the Secretariat, scheduled for completion by June 2018.

It was initially planned to construct the Secretariat on 32 acres of land north of Zia Uddyan and west of the Bangladesh-China Friendship International Conference Centre, where the annual trade fair is held. The plan followed the original blueprint by Louis I. Kahn, the architect of the National Parliament Building.

During the Awami League administration, the original designs of the entire Sher-e-Bangla Nagar including the National Parliament Building by American architect Louis I. Kahn were brought to the country at the cost of 400,000 dollars. The plan was to build four main buildings with nine floors on top of fourteen-story bases.

However, the relocation did not materialise. During the interim government period of one and a half years, there was no discussion about moving the Secretariat.

Under the new BNP government, a project was undertaken to construct a 21-story building within the Secretariat at a cost of Tk 6 billion. When the project was presented at an ECNEC meeting on 26 April, it was sent back without approval.

In the meeting, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman instructed the Ministry of Housing and Public Works and the Department of Architecture to assess the possibility of relocating the Secretariat to Sher-e-Bangla Nagar.

Project worth Tk 35 billion

In the past five months, the Ministry of Housing and Public Works has held several meetings with stakeholders regarding the potential relocation site for the Secretariat. The preliminary estimated cost for implementing the project is Tk 35 billion.

After five months of review, a report was presented in front of the Prime Minister last Wednesday. Three separate designs by three teams from the Department of Architecture were shown in the meeting. One design was finalised, and based on it, the Housing Department was instructed to prepare the project.

New roads and facilities

According to the proposed design, a circular road will surround the Secretariat. A road will be constructed behind the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Center. This road will exit to Mirpur Road passing by the July Uprising Museum (former Ganabhaban).

There are various establishments near the museum such as schools, hospitals, and the Ministry of Defence which may need to be relocated to accommodate this road.

The Ministry of Housing and Public Works has indicated discussions about constructing an underground road beneath the road that runs from Bijoy Sarani through Agargaon to Mirpur No. 10. The proposed Secretariat could be accessed via the upper road, while Mirpur Road can be reached using the lower road. A separate project might be undertaken for this.

According to the proposed design, each building within the Secretariat will be 12 stories tall. The buildings will be constructed in alignment with the National Parliament.

Related sources indicate that after the relocation of the Secretariat to Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, the main challenge will be traffic congestion. However, the Ministry of Housing and Public Works stated that measures will be taken to keep the area free from congestion.

A source from the Ministry of Housing and Public Works mentioned that after the Secretariat moves from Abdul Gani Road to Sher-e-Bangla Nagar, the current Secretariat could be repurposed for government offices such as the Dhaka Deputy Commissioner’s (DC) Office and the Superintendent of Police’s (SP) Office, currently scattered throughout Old Dhaka.

Due to limited space, the current Secretariat poses challenges for officials in carrying out office work effectively and causes heavy traffic congestion around it, leading to wasted working hours. The current Secretariat covers 1.7 million square feet, while the proposed design plans for a 3.1 million square feet area.

The trade fair ground belongs to the Ministry of Housing and Public Works, and the trade fair was moved to Purbachal in 2021, leaving the ground vacant. Four years ago, a project was undertaken to build a park on the vacant land at a cost of Tk 1 billion, although the project did not come to fruition.

Traffic congestion could be severe

The Ministry of Housing and Public Works believes that leaving the area vacant could lead to unauthorised occupation. If the Secretariat is relocated, it would prevent the land from being encroached upon.

Architect Iqbal Habib opines that relocating the Secretariat to Sher-e-Bangla Nagar following Louis I. Kahn's 1969 design would be inappropriate in 2026. He suggests considering alternative sites for relocation, similar to Putrajaya in Malaysia.

Iqbal Habib mentioned that numerous government facilities have already emerged in Sher-e-Bangla Nagar and Agargaon, increasing the number of vehicles in the area. Establishing the Secretariat there could lead to severe traffic congestion.

Health and Family Welfare Minister Sardar Md Sakhawat Husain has reaffirmed the government's commitment to gradually increase the health sector allocation to 5% of gross domestic product (GDP) and recruit 25,000 midwives into the public healthcare system over the next few years.
He made the remarks at a ministerial roundtable titled “Accelerating Midwifery and South-South Partnerships for Health Security: From Crisis to Resilience” in Berlin, Germany, on Sunday.
The health minister said midwives play a crucial role in ensuring safe, dignified and life-saving healthcare for mothers and newborns. They help improve antenatal care, safe childbirth, emergency referrals and postnatal services.
He said the government considers investment in midwives not an expense but a national investment that helps reduce maternal and newborn deaths and lower overall healthcare costs.
Sakhawat Husain said infrastructure at 62 educational institutions across the country was being modernized to improve the quality of midwifery education. Initiatives have also been taken to introduce hands-on training, simulation-based learning and technology-driven education.
The minister stressed the importance of regional cooperation in addressing the shortage of healthcare workers. Bangladesh is strengthening knowledge-sharing, faculty exchanges and joint training programs with Nepal and Pakistan, he said.
He also praised development partners, particularly the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA), for their contributions to expanding maternal and reproductive healthcare services.
Highlighting the role of midwives during climate-related disasters and humanitarian operations for Rohingya refugees in Cox's Bazar, the minister said they work on the front lines to ensure continuity of life-saving maternal healthcare during crises.
He reaffirmed the government's commitment to continued investment in midwives and strengthening their skills to protect women, children and the country's future economy.

item.title: 109 migrants dead, 116 missing in boat wreck off Djibouti
item.description:
At least 109 migrants died, including 15 children, and some 116 went missing when a boat sank off the shores of Djibouti overnight on October 8-9, a UN agency said Sunday.
Survivors said the vessel -- which was carrying 305 people from Djibouti to Yemen -- capsized north of the Djibouti town of Obock, according to a statement from the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
“This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives,” said Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, in the statement.
He said IOM teams were on the ground alongside Djiboutian authorities to provide emergency aid.
“This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities” by trying to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen and then to reach Gulf countries.
Among the 109 bodies recovered were 52 men, 42 women and 15 children -- nine girls and six boys -- the statement said.
More than 80 people survived the shipwreck, all Ethiopian nationals.
“Poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change drive many to undertake this journey, despite mounting instability across the Middle East,” the IOM said.
Yemen is stricken by fighting between the Saudi-backed government and Tehran-backed Houthi rebels, who have joined in the regional conflict involving the US and its allies against Iran.
IOM said it was assisting 64 survivors at a migrant centre in Obock.
“Djiboutian authorities are continuing search and rescue operations as fears grow for those still missing.”
Since September 10, the IOM detected more than 20,000 crossings to Djibouti from Ethiopia.
In 2025, more than 900 migrants died or went missing along the sea route to Yemen and the number attempting the journey increased by 18 percent, it said.
A shipwreck in March 2026 left nine people dead and 45 missing.
IOM spokesman Kennedy Omondi Okoth told AFP this week that most of the people attempting the journey were from Ethiopia or Somalia.
He said many of them were ending up stuck in Djibouti.
The IOM urged “donors and partners to strengthen support for Djibouti’s response, including search and rescue operations and life-saving assistance”.

item.title: Pennsylvania shooting kills 9, including suspect
item.description:
Nine people, including two young children and a pregnant woman, were killed in a shooting at a residence in Erie, Pennsylvania, on Friday, with the suspected gunman dying from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound, police said Saturday.
According to NBC News and USA TODAY, the victims included seven family members of the 45-year-old suspected shooter and a family friend. The victims ranged in age from 22 months to 51 years, according to police accounts.
Erie police received a gunshot detection alert at about 4:52pm Friday and responded to a residence on the 700 block of Perry Street. Police Chief Rick Lorah said officers arrived about three minutes after the alert and found two women, aged 51 and 37, fatally wounded outside the house.
Investigators reviewing a neighbour’s doorbell camera footage found that the women appeared distressed as they approached the residence and knocked on the door seeking assistance. Audio from the footage appeared to capture muffled gunfire from inside the house before the suspect came outside and shot the women as they ran towards him, Lorah said.
The suspect then returned inside the residence. Police reported no further gunshots after officers arrived.
Officers initially could not establish contact with anyone inside the house. According to a statement from the Erie city government cited by USA TODAY, police secured the area before a special weapons and tactics (SWAT) team entered and cleared the residence.
The officers initially saw no movement inside and heard no gunshots or cries for help. Police said they had limited information about whether the suspect remained inside or posed an ongoing threat. The city clarified that the deaths occurred before officers entered the house and that the incident did not involve a prolonged standoff or a delay caused by obtaining a search warrant.
After deploying a robot to assess the scene, officers entered the residence and found several victims. A 5-year-old boy and a 22-month-old girl were found on the first floor, while four other victims — women aged 24 and 44 and men aged 19 and 21 — were discovered in a stairwell on the second floor.
The suspected shooter, a 45-year-old man whose identity had not been publicly released, was found dead on the second floor. Police recovered a .40-caliber handgun registered to him, Lorah said.
One of the victims found inside the house was eight months pregnant. Police said the victims found inside lived at the residence, while the two women killed outside did not. One of the women was a family friend, while the other was related to a family member, according to police accounts.
Erie County Coroner Lyell Cook said his office was working to confirm the identities of the deceased. Authorities had not publicly released their names or announced final determinations on the causes of death as of Saturday afternoon, USA TODAY reported.
Lorah described the scene as the worst he had encountered during his law enforcement career. He said investigators were examining evidence, reviewing cellphones and interviewing relatives and witnesses to establish what led to the shooting.
Although the police chief said mental health could be a factor, he stressed that investigators had not established a motive. He also noted that police had previously had contact with the suspected shooter, with the last interaction he recalled occurring in 2022.
Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro said he had spoken with Erie Mayor Daria Devlin and offered the state government’s support to the victims’ families and the wider community.
“My heart breaks for this family,” Shapiro wrote on social media, adding that he and his wife were praying for the victims’ loved ones and the Erie community.
Devlin said the city was coordinating with crisis services, behavioural health providers, schools and community organisations to provide support to affected residents. Erie County District Attorney Elizabeth Hirz also urged the public to avoid spreading rumours and unverified information while the investigation continues.
The shooting occurred on the same weekend that two Philadelphia police officers were shot early Saturday. Shapiro described the incidents as a dark day for Pennsylvania.
Erie is located about 190 kilometres north of Pittsburgh.

item.title: Flash flood sweeps away 65 houses in Nepal, 5 missing
item.description:
Five people are missing after a flash flood swept away 65 houses and damaged four bridges along Nepal’s Budhi Gandaki River in the central part of the country on Sunday, according to reports by AP.
The flood struck Gorkha and Dhading districts after a landslide at Chumanubri Rural Municipality in Gorkha temporarily blocked the river, according to the Nepal Army. The river later breached the blockage, sending a sudden surge of water, mud, and debris through settlements along its banks.
Armed Police Force spokesperson Netra Bahadur Karki said all five missing people were reported from Gorkha district, adding that authorities were still collecting information about the extent of the damage.
The flood destroyed two motorable bridges and two suspension bridges, disrupting local connectivity.
The Nepal Army airlifted 36 people to safer locations following the disaster, while security forces continued search and rescue operations.
The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority evacuated residents from vulnerable areas and urged people living nearby to move to safer locations. Authorities also warned residents to remain vigilant as the situation developed.
Videos circulating on social media showed floodwaters rushing through steep mountain valleys, carrying away houses and other structures. The full extent of the damage and the number of affected settlements remained unclear.
The flooding also raised concerns in Arughat, a riverside town along a highway connecting Kathmandu with other parts of the country, where social media posts indicated that warnings had prompted evacuations.
The Budhi Gandaki River flows into the Trishuli River, an important waterway near Nepal’s capital, Kathmandu.
The disaster comes as Nepal continues to recover from devastating floods in August along its mountainous border with China, which reportedly left more than 1,400 people dead and thousands missing.
Prime Minister Balendra Shah’s office subsequently announced the end of search and rescue operations for additional victims of the earlier disaster, with authorities shifting their focus to recovery and reconstruction. Damaged roads and bridges, particularly in remote areas, have hampered the delivery of relief supplies.
The government estimates that reconstruction following the earlier floods will cost $4.77 billion. Nearly 33,000 people were affected, while about 7,500 houses were damaged or destroyed.

item.title: The Trump administration just cut down a century’s worth of history at a D.C. golf course
item.description:
Workers removed more than 500 trees over the weekend at a Washington, D.C., golf course that President Donald Trump is working to remodel. It happened like many of his other design projects around town: suddenly and without permission.

Preservationists asked a judge Sunday to halt the Trump administration after it removed 529 trees Saturday at East Potomac Park, a golf course managed by the National Park Service, and on Monday, a judge called the removal “inexcusable.”

The course is home to elms, oaks, pines, and willows, as well as some of the 3,000 Japanese flowering cherry trees gifted by the government of Japan in 1912. Together they told the story of golf’s rise in America from a mostly treeless game on the U.S. coasts to a sport known for its big, lush vegetation. Now, just like that, a century’s worth of landscape design history has been torn up.

The removal happened “faster than anticipated,” according to the lawsuit, and the Trump administration didn’t meet its obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act, attorneys representing the D.C. Preservation League and a pair of local golfers said in a filing seeking an emergency action to pause further tree removal.

“‘Pulling a fast one’ has become the model this administration uses to circumvent the laws intended to protect the environment and D.C. landmarks,” Abbe D. Lowell, a founding member of Lowell & Associates, which is representing the plaintiffs along with Democracy Forward and Democracy Defenders Fund, said in a statement. “It did so with the East Wing and the Kennedy Center, and we are continuing our effort to stop them before they succeed in destroying D.C.’s historic public golf course.”

A brief history of parkland courses

East Potomac Park sits on a small island in the Potomac River, just south of the National Mall. Its earliest known vegetation consisted of tall grass and willow trees, most of which were cleared to design the first golf course in 1917. Over the years, more trees were added to adapt to changing tastes, according to a 2017 cultural landscape inventory of the course conducted by the Urban Heritage Project from the University of Pennsylvania’s Stuart Weitzman School of Design.

The first course at East Potomac Park was designed by golf course architect Walter J. Travis, who cleared the fairways of most willows but kept some existing trees along the course’s perimeter to separate the front and back nine. A new style of golf course design in the 1920s called parkland style, however, meant more trees would eventually be planted over the years.

As golf grew more popular and moved inland, parkland courses came to be known for their big, mature trees. The popularity of televised golf tournaments beginning in the 1950s and ’60s only made lush, green, gorgeous park-like backdrops that more appealing, according to the inventory, like the Masters Tournament in Augusta, Georgia, with its trees and plants imported from around the world in bloom.

At East Potomac Park, the Civilian Conservation Corps planted cedar trees in 1939 and additional trees in the 1960s and ’70s, including crab apple trees. The 2017 inventory also counted large wolf trees, large willow oaks, and a large American elm.

Some trees were planted for reasons of gameplay, not just aesthetics. The park’s miniature golf course, for example, was designed around a limited number of trees that function as hazards, and the park’s White Course has few trees and open fairways, making it popular with less competitive players.

The 2017 inventory noted that the park needed some care, including clearing invasive vines and trees that were were damaging some of the cherry trees. It also said that a “piecemeal nature of planting” had resulted in “a variety of mature trees and shrubs scattered throughout the landscape” that had no overall harmony.

A “surprise demolition”

But those suing Trump’s Interior Department and National Park Service say the administration’s tree razing went far above routine maintenance or a thoughtful pruning, and that the administration had even removed healthy, mature oaks and maple trees.

“Unleashing a surprise demolition razing over 500 historic trees in this public park and claiming it is part of maintenance from a dated, years-old landscaping plan is yet another brazen, lawless power grab that has become routine for the Trump administration,” Democracy Defenders Fund executive chair Norm Eisen said in a statement.

Trump’s planned makeover of the park (he had rubble from the White House’s East Wing demolition taken there) is part of a larger takeover of the federal government golf course system. Trump is reportedly offering his Trump International Golf Club West Palm Beach in Florida as an official U.S. government golf course for presidents that his family’s company would continue to operate.

Like the rings of a tree tell its story, the landscape design of East Potomac Park told a story of a game that grew up to appreciate the value of mature trees and ample vegetation as it became more popular. With the Trump administration’s sudden tree removal, part of that history is now gone.

item.title: Congress wants to keep AM radio in every new car
item.description:
In the era of streaming music and satellite radio, traditional broadcast stations are easy to overlook. AM radio, in particular, has fallen out of favor with younger drivers. So it’s perhaps no surprise that some automakers have begun dropping it from new vehicles. Congress, however, wants to put a stop to that.

Last month, the U.S. House of Representatives passed H.R. 979, the “AM Radio for Every Vehicle Act of 2025.” The bill is now on the Senate’s legislative calendar and has broad bipartisan support. The Senate also has a companion bill, S. 315, which cleared committee last year and is awaiting a floor vote.

While AM radio is dominated by political talk shows, religious programming, and sports, it still draws a sizable audience. The National Association of Broadcasters (NAB), which supports the congressional effort, says more than 80 million Americans listen to AM each month.

The group describes AM radio as “a platform for locally produced content that is relevant to their audience and speaks to their unique cultural and linguistic needs.” It also notes that AM stations have historically provided an entry point into radio ownership for racial and ethnic minorities.

Automakers, meanwhile, are grappling with tariffs and rising component costs, and looking for ways to trim expenses. Removing AM radio wouldn’t shave hundreds or thousands of dollars off a vehicle’s price, but it could offer modest savings.

Electric vehicle makers face another challenge: The technology that powers EVs can interfere with AM radio reception.

“The high-voltage electrical systems in EVs generate electromagnetic interference that, according to the Center for Automotive Research, ‘distorts AM radio signals, affecting the listening experience for drivers and passengers.’ In other words: really staticky,” said John Bozzella, president and CEO of the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, in 2024 congressional testimony. “It’s not possible to eliminate that interference, and techniques to reduce interference add weight and mess with battery range and would cost an estimated $3.8 billion.”

Bozzella also argued that requiring AM radio amounted to a government mandate with no public safety justification.

Supporters of the legislation dispute that argument. AM stations play a significant role in the nation’s emergency alert infrastructure, including a FEMA-supported network of radio stations equipped to continue broadcasting during disasters.

Bozzella’s position was echoed by the then-president and CEO of the Consumer Technology Association, who wrote in a letter to the editor of The Washington Post that “a federal mandate that every car comes equipped with an AM radio in 2024 and beyond is like mandating that they come equipped with ashtrays or 8-track players.”

Still, traditional radio may have more life left in it than skeptics think, even as music streaming subscriptions approach 1 billion worldwide.

As more Americans return to the office, radio has benefited from renewed interest. Edison Research’s “Share of Ear” report, released in July, found that AM/FM radio accounted for 62% of ad-supported audio listening among adults, compared with just 6% for Spotify’s ad-supported service. In cars, AM/FM commanded an even larger share of ad-supported audio listening: 82% among adults 18 and older.

Whether the Senate will vote on the AM radio bill before November’s midterm elections remains unclear. And despite its bipartisan support, its prospects at the White House are uncertain.

The auto industry may oppose the measure, but it has some influential backers beyond the broadcasting industry, including the American Farm Bureau Federation, AARP, and a coalition of public safety organizations.

item.title: Elon Musk quietly becomes the biggest donor in the midterms in a bid to save Republicans
item.description:
Elon Musk, the world’s only trillionaire, has quietly become the biggest known donor in this year’s midterm elections, doling out more than $276 million since July to try to save Republican majorities in Congress.

The numbers, first reported by The New York Times ahead of this week’s federal filing deadline, were confirmed by Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for Musk’s super PAC.

The money includes $158 million given to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC supporting Republican Senate candidates, one of the largest known political donations in American history, according to the Times.

Another $76 million went to America PAC, a Musk super PAC, which has once again built out a major turnout operation like the one it used to help elect President Donald Trump by knocking on doors in 2024.

Musk also provided $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, a group that supports the Republican nominee for Senate in Texas, Ken Paxton. The race has been a major focus of Musk’s efforts.

It’s a dramatic turnaround since last May, when Musk said he intended to cut back on future political spending. “I think I’ve done enough,” he said at the time.

Despite the cash infusion, Musk has generally kept a lower profile than in 2024, when he appeared onstage next to Trump at rallies, and in the early days of the president’s second term, when he led the Department of Government Efficiency.

He had a falling out with Trump while leaving his government post, but the two have since reconciled. Trump presented Musk with the National Medal of Science last week.

Musk’s net worth has fluctuated around the trillion-dollar line this year based on changes in stock prices, but he topped $1 trillion again last week according to Forbes magazine.

Republicans have a gaping financial advantage over their Democratic counterparts—a disparity that has been a rare bright spot for a party that is bracing for major potential losses amid deep voter frustration over the president’s performance, stubbornly high prices, and the unpopular war with Iran.

They have been using the money to blanket the airwaves in the race’s final stretch.

“These robust investments have allowed the GOP apparatus to get its message out so Republicans can have a fighting chance to defy history,” Romeo told the Times.

Democrats responded to the news by accusing Republicans of using vast amounts of cash to mask their shortcomings.

“Republicans are hoping to buy these elections, injecting tens of millions into races to try and outrun their unpopular candidates, unpopular president, and unpopular economy,” said Lauren French, a spokesperson for Democrats’ Senate Majority PAC.

—By Jill Colvin, Associated Press

item.title: Subterranean Warfare - An Urgent DoW Need Without An Owner
item.description:
The DoW urgently needs to organize its scattered subterranean warfare assets into a single unified organization. Ideally, a Direct Reporting Portfolio Manager (DRPM) for Subterranean Warfare, reporting to the Deputy Secretary of War. (The Department already uses this model for unmanned systems, critical weapons and Golden Dome.) This group would have three portfolios: Subterranean Resilience, Subterranean Sensing and Subterranean Defeat. The office would integrate validated requirements, experimentation, testing, acquisition, and fielding.

Subterranean Resilience

During the 2026 Iran conflict, Iranian ballistic missiles and low-cost drones hit U.S. installations across eight Middle Eastern countries. Hundreds of buildings and structures were damaged or destroyed. The Navy’s Fifth Fleet headquarters in Bahrain was among the installations hit hard. Iranian weapons damaged one E-3 airborne early-warning aircraft and five KC-135 tankers on the ground in Saudi Arabia. (The official inspector-general report documents the damage.) Despite thousands of successful interceptions, the attacks exposed the vulnerability of concentrated, above-ground assets.

The rapid redeployment of the B-1s from RAF Fairford in the UK after warnings of an Iran-linked threat (reported as a possible drone attack) made the point: unsheltered concentrated high-value aircraft are vulnerable even way outside the theater.

The assumptions the U.S. has made about air superiority, missile defense, aircraft dispersal, building hardening, and the survivability of concentrated forward bases were all flawed. While we were prepared for ballistic missiles and hostile aircraft, drone swarms combined with ballistic missiles saturated and got through our defenses.

Washington’s reaction has been to invest billions of dollars in counter-drone and missile defense systems. Yet public budget documents reveal no comparable effort to put vulnerable aircraft, fuel, command-and-control nodes, and munitions out of harm’s way – sheltered, underground (or in space). (Agile Combat Employment, dispersal, hardening, deception, shelters, and rapid runway repair were never designed for a combined drone and missile onslaught.)

The Pentagon has recognized for decades that underground facilities are among the most effective ways an adversary can blunt U.S. conventional superiority. It described that problem explicitly in 1999. Gaza and Ukraine should have made it abundantly clear.

China, Russia, North Korea, and Iran use underground facilities, dispersal, hardening, and deception to make their own high-value assets harder to find, assess, and disable. We need to underground assets that cannot be quickly replaced: command posts, comms nodes, ammunition, fuel distribution points, repair facilities, key power systems, maintenance spares, and high-value aircraft or drones. The department needs an integrator that coordinates resilience across the Military Departments, Joint Staff, combatant commands, defense agencies, and intelligence community and provides Subterranean Resilience.

However, resilience is only one part of subterranean warfare.

Subterranean Sensing and Defeat

The U.S. needs to know where adversaries' underground facilities are located, and the internal layout of those facilities. Today, these bespoke exquisite systems for tunnel detection, robotic mapping of accessible tunnels, Hard and Deeply Buried Targets (HDBT) characterization, and target defeat are siloed in organizations scattered across the DoW. Most of these systems still require boots on the ground. Once a target is found, Combatant Commands need an integrated system that can characterize and destroy these targets, without first gaining physical access. Today, for the deepest facilities that means bombing from the air. Iran is the case in point.

Background. Iran's route to a nuclear weapon is by enriching uranium. Natural uranium is composed of 0.71% uranium-235 (U235) and it’s only the U235 that is used to build a bomb.

Iran uses centrifuges to separate U235 and increase its concentration (enriching it.) One centrifuge won’t do much, but connecting thousands of centrifuges together into cascades and running them for months can produce pounds of U235.

Iran’s underground nuclear enrichment site at Natanz had well over 10,000 centrifuges installed across dozens of cascades, and their Fordow nuclear enrichment site was built for 16 cascades, roughly 3,000 machines. Before the June 2025 strikes, Iran’s three declared enrichment facilities contained more than 20,000 centrifuges in 125 full-sized cascades.

The rough estimate needed for one Iranian nuclear weapon is ~100 lbs of U-235 at 60% enrichment or 55 lbs of U-235 at 90% enrichment (modern designs use less.) The difference is important, the lighter the weapon the easier it is to fit on a missile.

At its peak (Feb 2025 to June 2025) Iran’s cascades were delivering ~86 lbs of uranium enriched to 60% which is about 50 lbs of U-235 per month, which is just under one potential weapon every month. (Most weapons use U235 enriched to 90+% because that permits a smaller, more reliable design. Getting to that level in Iran might take days or weeks running the cascades, but building it into a weapon would still be needed.)

Deeply Buried Targets Versus Bunker Busters. One of the stated goals of the U.S. strikes on Iran was to remove their capacity to build nuclear weapons. This required the U.S. to destroy their deeply buried underground nuclear enrichment sites. The largest conventional bomb in the U.S. military’s arsenal is the 30,000-pound GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator, carried by the B-2 Bomber. A 2019 description said it could reach targets as far as 200 feet underground (its actual effectiveness depends on geology, concrete, facility design, entry points, and the use of multiple weapons). The Iranians knew this and built their nuclear enrichment sites underground. The Fordow site is ~260 to 300 feet under limestone and dolomite. The Natanz site is 25 to 160 feet underground, protected by a 25-foot concrete shield. (But public estimates are over the place.)

Iran declared Isfahan as an enrichment complex to the IAEA the day before the June 2025 strikes; inspectors never got inside it, therefore its depth and geology are unknown, but speculation is that the enrichment complex is 260 to 330 feet underground. Another suspected enrichment facility is in Pickaxe Mountain, where the exact depths, geology, are unknown but estimates put the facility 250 – 330 feet below the summit. Both Isfahan and Pickaxe were Iran’s shift toward "deep mountain basing" to escape the reach of conventional military strikes.

In June 2025 in Operation Midnight Hammer U.S. B-2 bombers dropped 14 GBU-57 bombs on top of Fordow and Natanz. At Isfahan (Esfahan) more than two-dozen submarine-launched Tomahawks hit tunnel entrances and surface targets. In March 2026, strikes at Natanz hit its entrance.

According to the Institute for Science and International Security, the 22,000 centrifuges at Natanz, the Natanz pilot plant, and Fordow are almost certainly wrecked. What may have survived is the enriched uranium, the spare parts, and the people, and that is the problem. The International Atomic Energy Agency estimated (in June 2025) that Iran had about 970 pounds of uranium enriched to 60%; it has since lost track of where it is. Iran's known uranium conversion capability at Isfahan was damaged, which it needed to turn the stockpile of enriched uranium into a weapon, and there is no public evidence that enrichment has resumed at Natanz, Fordow or Isfahan. We never hit Pickaxe Mountain or the Isfahan enrichment facility with the GBU-57. The strikes have set Iran back, but no one knows for how long.

While the GBU-57 MOP cannot cleanly punch through solid rock, the debate has shifted from an absolute physical destruction calculation to a functional denial calculation—meaning the military's goal would be to seal Iran's nuclear assets in a mountain tomb rather than blowing them up directly.

Did We Succeed? Our stated goal was to prevent Iran from rapidly rebuilding the capability to build nuclear weapons, but there’s no certainty that we did that. Repeated airstrikes may have damaged the buried enrichment plants, but we can’t prove it or account for the buried enriched uranium inside. The fact is that it’s extremely difficult to see how much damage the bombs did to Hard and Deeply Buried Targets (HDBTs) from the air, and without inspectors on the ground, knowing for sure is guesswork. Putting boots on the ground would carry enormous costs and risks. Negotiating the removal and inspection of weapons grade uranium would depend on Iranian cooperation and a way to verify we got it all. All bad choices.

There is another emerging option: autonomous drilling equipment.

Subterranean Sensing and Defeat. It’s not hard to imagine that with enough boots on the ground the U.S. could secure a landing zone, fly in drilling equipment and have crews drill hundreds of feet vertically or thousands horizontally to either place sensors and/or explosives. The U.S. has had organizations building specialized equipment and training for breaching tunnels in Combatant Commands and scattered across the DoW for years (DTRA, DARPA, Army ERDC and CAVES and CZ5 programs, SOCOM, Sandia and the Army's half-billion-dollar underground-training push (2018) and ATP 3-21.51 Subterranean Operations.) One can even imagine that there are teams already trained and equipment ready to go. And one can equally imagine the Iranians are waiting for them.

What’s new is autonomous drills that could provide post-strike bomb damage assessments and/or destroy Hard and Deeply Buried Targets (HDBTs) without seizing the site. They might be inserted covertly; more likely they'd need air cover while they work.

The combination of AI, robotics and autonomy moves this from science fiction to the possible.

Anduril, The Boring Company, Exodigo, Phoenix Boring, Earthgrid and Traysar are possible candidates to deliver these systems. There are likely others as well.

(Disclosure: after my first blog about undergrounding critical assets, I invested and have a financial interest in companies in this space.)

Surface survivability and subterranean sensing and defeat are no longer one Service's problem, and they won't be solved by a single system or an incremental fix. Something fundamentally disruptive has changed in the nature of asymmetric warfare and there’s no going back. While we’re actively chasing immediate solutions (Golden Dome, JIATF-401, et al), we need to rethink the nature of force protection, and military and civilian infrastructure protection.

The U.S. needs a coherent protection and survivability strategy across the DoW and all sectors of our economy. This conversation needs to be not only about how we do it, but how we organize it, how we budget and pay for it, and how we rapidly deploy it.

item.title: The Sanctions We Cannot Afford
item.description:
On the evening of Friday, October 9, the Treasury published General License 135. It authorizes the “sale, delivery, offloading and importation” of Russian diesel until April 7, 2027, and does not specify a buyer, a seller, or a quantity. The President provided the quantities after a call with President Putin: more than 300,000 tons “immediately,” 500,000 in November, and millions more if Russia’s refineries allow. The first shipment amounts to less than a day of American consumption. The shipment comes from a country that barred its own diesel exports in July and, in the last quarter, imported the fuel for the first time. AAA put the national average for diesel that day at $6.28 a gallon.

The license is valid for six months. The law beside it allows nine days. On September 18, the President signed a sanctions act that the Senate had passed 86-11. By October 18, it requires duties of up to 500 percent on Russian goods and duties of up to 100 percent on every export to the United States from any of the five largest importers of Russian crude oil or natural gas that knowingly purchases again. The first duty covers petroleum products, and so the diesel the Treasury has just licensed. A third law, passed in 2022 and never repealed, still bars Russian petroleum from American ports; the license does not mention it. Washington must penalize Russia’s customers nine days after licensing itself to become one.

For six weeks in these pages, I have argued that the United States is assembling the instruments of great-power competition without deciding who commands them. This week, the pattern reached the oldest instrument of economic warfare, the sanction, and it was not only an American pattern.

On October 7, the European Union’s ambassadors agreed on their 22nd package of sanctions against Russia. They removed one Russian company at Estonia’s request because it supplies the rare earths that an Estonian plant refines for European magnets. Two days later, in Beijing, the European trade commissioner announced an understanding under which China will moderate its exports of hybrid cars to Europe. In return, Beijing will continue to process European companies’ rare-earth and magnet licenses through what both sides call a green channel. The notice suspending China’s licensing rules for American buyers still expires on paper on November 10, eight days before the President is due in Shenzhen. The United States received no such channel.

China’s rare-earth controls are administered by a single ministry, which this week rewarded Europe while leaving the United States waiting. That is an exception used as an instrument: a favor granted in exchange for a concession, and revocable. The American and European exceptions were of another kind. They were relief from sanctions the governments had imposed themselves, granted because the price of diesel or a factory’s feedstock had become intolerable. An exception of that kind is information. It tells Moscow and Beijing the price at which the pressure on them will be lifted.

Each of the week’s decisions had a reason its government could defend. Diesel at more than six dollars a gallon before winter is a real problem, and so is a processing plant in a frontline state of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. But a sanction lasts only as long as its author can go without what it forbids.

The difficulty is that each decision was made by the office responsible for a single problem. The Treasury issues the license; the President sets the duties, and the Trade Representative adjusts them afterward. The fuel Russia has promised comes from refineries Ukraine is striking, so every Ukrainian strike now reduces the diesel Washington has announced, and Moscow has a commercial reason to ask the United States to restrain Kyiv. The President had already asked Kyiv in September to “take it easy on the refineries,” and President Zelensky called the license “a weak decision by strong partners.” No single authority beneath the President is charged with weighing one of these decisions against another before it reaches him. Each office did its work, and the claim that prevailed was the one with the nearest deadline.

The United States has faced this problem before. In July 1943, after a public quarrel between the board planning economic warfare and the agency financing it, President Roosevelt abolished the board. By September, he had placed economic warfare, lend-lease, and foreign relief under a single Foreign Economic Administration. He did so in the middle of a war because instruments that pull against one another need someone with the authority to rank them.

The duties due on October 18 are the place to begin, and they will be easy to read. A real duty on Russian goods and on Russia’s customers restores the sanction, and taxes the diesel Washington asked for. A nominal rate satisfies the statute and confirms the license as the policy. A waiver says so outright. In the last two cases, Russia’s customers may conclude that buying is safe, and Beijing that American pressure has a price that can be quoted in advance.

Avoiding that takes two things the West has not arranged. The first is a single authority who can rank the claims before they reach the President and hold every office to that ranking: someone who decides whether the sanction yields to the price of diesel or the price of diesel yields to the sanction. The second is provision. A sanction is a siege, and a siege is won by the side that can wait. A government that means to forbid a thing should first establish what it will need from the adversary while the prohibition lasts, then stockpile it, find it elsewhere, or grant the exception at the outset on its own terms.

If you advise on these decisions, ask for the ranking before the duties are signed and for the provisions before the next sanction is drafted. Otherwise, Moscow and Beijing will read October 18 as a schedule of American needs, with the dates on which they fall due.

item.title: What Beijing Calls Open, Washington Should Call an Operation
item.description:
China is about to run the largest influence operation in history. It will not have to run it. The world will download it.

Our research team at Vanderbilt spent months inside the internal documents of GoLaxy, a Beijing firm with ties to the Chinese state. It built a machine for shaping opinion in other countries: A.I. that generates personas, amplifies the stories Beijing wants believed and buries the ones it does not. It was used in Hong Kong. It was used in Taiwan. That is an influence operation built by hand, one persona at a time.

Now consider what happens when it does not need to be built at all. If Chinese open-weight models — the ones anyone can download, modify and run on their own machines — become the foundation the world builds on, the Party's framing of Taiwan, Tiananmen, Xinjiang and Beijing itself ships inside every product that sits on top. No personas. No campaign. Just the default answer, everywhere. GoLaxy would look like a rehearsal.

Here is the part that should stop Washington cold. Chinese models are about to be everywhere, and American strategy is what is putting them there.

Washington is deciding whether to let frontier development run while clamping down on powerful open-weight models whose safeguards can be stripped away. Restrictions would not kill demand for a cheap model a company can download and make its own. China is standing at the counter with exactly that.

We talk about the A.I. race as if it has one finish line. It has two. The first is for frontier capability: who builds the most advanced models. American companies lead today. The second is for reach: whose models become the foundation under thousands of products. Chinese firms may be building the advantage there. The first brings concentrated scientific, economic and military power. The second decides whose systems become the workhorses of ordinary life, and that reach shapes what people know.

American frontier models such as Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini are closed: you use them on the company's servers, and the company can cut off access. Chinese developers compete by releasing cheap open-weight models that companies can run on their own, with no provider to answer to.

This has already started. Airbnb relies on Alibaba's Qwen in its customer-service agent. Qwen even briefly powered a tool for searching proposed regulations on the Federal Register website. Amazon says thousands of customers have deployed DeepSeek through its cloud. In every case the interface is American. The model underneath is not.

Chinese developers operate under Communist Party rules about what may be said. Those rules shape which questions the models answer, which facts they omit and how they frame sensitive subjects. Open weights can be retuned, but scrubbing built-in defaults is expensive, and most companies will tune what matters to their business rather than check how a model handles every political subject. If a cheap Chinese model sits under thousands of products, its habits travel with it — into research tools, classroom software and fact-checkers — and the person on the other end never knows.

Beijing already believes this. When Meta released its open-weight Llama models, Chinese regulators worried that a foreign model could "poison" China's A.I. ecosystem with information the Party censors. Washington should take seriously a vulnerability Beijing recognized first.

None of this makes the open-weight safety problem smaller. It makes it bigger. Once a powerful open-weight model is out, its developer cannot recall it. Its safeguards can be stripped and the model turned toward cyberattacks, biological weapons or worse. Testing requirements, liability rules and release restrictions are needed. But a Chinese open-weight model carries the same dangerous capabilities as an American one, and no American rule touches it.

Constrain American developers and leave foreign weights untouched, and demand shifts toward Chinese models. Washington ends up regulating the companies it can see while deepening its dependence on the ones it cannot.

Washington could ban the Chinese models. But that means telling Americans which information technology they may use — and here lies the irony: the openness that protects Americans from domestic censorship may leave them exposed to systems built under Chinese censorship.

TikTok offers a glimpse of the stakes. More than 150 million Americans use it, and more than 50 million regularly get news there. Add DeepSeek or Qwen to generate the content TikTok’s algorithm selects and distributes, and China could supply both the information and the system that delivers it to an enormous audience.

The United States therefore faces a trilemma. It wants to prevent the uncontrolled release of dangerous A.I. capabilities. It wants to preserve Americans' freedom to choose their technology and information. And it wants to avoid dependence on models shaped inside an authoritarian system. It cannot fully secure all three.

Honest regulation starts by admitting that. Before restricting an American model, ask which model developers will pick instead. Domestic and foreign models distributed in the United States should face the same tests and the same rules. And companies that build products on a foundation model should have to say whose model it is.

A.I. leadership is two things: the capability of a country's best models, and the reach of the models embedded in ordinary life. A.I. risk is two things as well: what a powerful model might do, and what a ubiquitous one tells people is true. GoLaxy showed what Beijing does with a machine for shaping belief. Open weights are how it gets one in every pocket. And right now, Washington is holding the door.

Mr. Goldstein and Mr. Benson are professors at Vanderbilt University who specialize in national and international security.
